 Art professor uses talent to build relationships with community
 November 20, 2026 
 By Elizabeth Clarke, LCU News
 PINEVILLE, La. (LBM) – Hannah Fulton, an assistant professor of art at Louisiana Christian University, believes community involvement is key to creating a successful artist and a successful art program.
 Fulton, a Sabine Parish native, began teaching at LCU in 2022, after completing her Master of Fine Arts with an emphasis in studio painting and drawing at Louisiana Tech University in 2021. She earned her undergraduate degree in graphic communication with a minor in photography in 2016 at Northwestern State University.
 Before joining the faculty at LCU, she taught art for a year at the Louisiana School for Math, Science and the Arts in Natchitoches.
 Her love of art, however, is lifelong. And she got it honestly. Her father, Rodney Fulton, earned his degree in advertising and design.
 “I can remember drawing doodles and illustrations even in first grade,” she said.
 Her teacher gave the class prompts to write about in something she called The Daily Journal, she said.
 “We were given prompts to write, and I’d illustrate every entry,” Fulton said.
 By second grade, she was in essence taking elementary school “commissions.”
 “I would draw things for my classmates,” she said. “Someone would say, ‘hey, can you draw me a teddy bear’?”
 Fulton said she began very early, entering art contests, including a poster competition in the fourth grade for the Young Authors and Artists Contest, then sponsored by Sabine Parish.
 Her love and her talent continued to blossom, and in college she participated in several student art exhibitions.
 By graduate school at Northwestern, her work was in high demand—literally. Fulton had a painting chosen to be featured on a billboard marketing the North Central Louisiana Arts Council. Someone in the community saw her “Honeybee” painting while passing by the billboard one day, and the person tracked her down and bought the original work.
 From honeybees to mystical creatures, Fulton sees the world in a rather colorful, fantastical, yet innocent way.
 “I want to do very unconventional things,” she said.
 Two years ago, she and a class of students painted the ceiling of the children’s area at Martin Branch of the Rapides Library System in Pineville. Colorful dragons soar over the visitors as they read and play.
 LCU studio art alumna Sam Miller was a student who participated in that project.
 “Hannah’s an exceptional artist and professor,” she said. “I always enjoyed art critique days in her classes because I would always get constructive criticism back, which would help me further improve and develop my skills.”
 Fulton prides herself on getting students to create work that will reach far outside the classroom. Community involvement drives her.
 In the variety of art courses she teaches, her students are not only working on drawing and painting, but on doing things with a specific purpose in mind, she said. They may be creating advertising and logo designs for branding, working on copy for a public service announcement, or simply learning how to manipulate design software in new and unique ways.
 “Hannah Fulton is a very knowledgeable art teacher who gives great insight on improving her art students’ work to prepare them for working in the real world of identity design,” said Victoria Gaspard, a junior graphic design major from Many. “She uses history to give pointers on how to make paintings, logos, etc. better for potential company use in the future.’
 In addition to getting her students’ work out there in the community, she believes it benefits LCU, as well.
 “Some in Louisiana still are not aware that LCU is here and that we have an art department, she said.”
 She said her goal for this semester was to put her own art out there, as well. She has joined a monthly community group of artists who meet at the Alexandria Museum of Art.
 She, her artist colleague Michael Smith, and three students have had work chosen for the River Oaks Square Arts Center’s 11th Annual Show. 
 Fulton also had work displayed at the Art, Jazz and Jambalaya Exhibition at the Centennial Cultural Center in Olla on the Saturday after Thanksgiving. 
 “There are lots of talented people in Central Louisiana and lots of talented, blessed students,” Fulton said. “And I want them to know LCU is here, and we have an art department—visual arts and graphic design. It’s a really good place to practice your craft.”
 For more information about art programs at LCU, visit LCU’s art and graphic design web page.
